signal_type: Beat-to-beat RR intervals exported via Garmin FitCSVTool and Movesense HR+ vs 3-lead criterion ECG
decomposition: Beat-to-beat R-peak detection sensitivity/precision and RR interval Bland-Altman agreement analysis
parameters_reported: R-peak sensitivity, precision, Pearson correlation r, and Bland-Altman mean bias ± SD at rest and during exercise
sampling_resampling: Raw beat-to-beat RR intervals extracted from Garmin .FIT files via FitCSVTool without interpolation prior to beat matching
band_definitions: Beat-to-beat RR interval domain (ms) supporting downstream time- and frequency-domain HRV
key_finding: At rest, Garmin HRM-Pro beat-to-beat RR intervals showed small mean bias (-8.5 ms, SD 111.5 ms) relative to 3-lead ECG, but high-intensity running degraded R-peak sensitivity (84.7%) and correlation (r = 0.66), underscoring the necessity of artifact filtering in wearable BBI pipelines.
device: Garmin HRM-Pro (logged via Garmin .FIT / FitCSVTool) and Movesense HR+
reference_standard: 3-lead laboratory ECG criterion
agreement_metric: Garmin HRM-Pro: R-peak sensitivity 84.7%, precision 87.7%, resting RR mean bias -8.5 ms (SD 111.5 ms), incremental test r = 0.66; Movesense HR+: sensitivity 99.7%, precision 99.6%, resting bias 0.23 ms (SD 22.3 ms), incremental r = 0.98

citation: Baek HJ, Cho CH, Cho J, Woo JM. Reliability of ultra-short-term analysis as a surrogate of standard 5-min analysis of heart rate variability. Telemed J E Health. 2015;21(5):404-414.
design: Cross-sectional methodological validation study across age-stratified healthy volunteers (n=467, aged 8-69 years)
signal_type: Resting 5-min PPG/ECG interbeat interval recordings sub-segmented into 11 ultra-short durations (10 to 270 s)
decomposition: Time-domain and parametric/non-parametric frequency-domain PSD across progressive recording window lengths
parameters_reported: Mean HR, SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50, VLF, LF, HF, LFn, HFn, and LF/HF ratio across 10 s to 300 s windows
sampling_resampling: Spline interpolation and resampling of beat-to-beat intervals across window lengths from 10 s up to 300 s
key_finding: Established minimum recording durations to validly reproduce standard 5-min HRV: 10 s for HR, 20 s for HF, 30 s for RMSSD, 60 s for pNN50, 90 s for LF/LFn/HFn/LF:HF, 240 s for SDNN, and >=270 s for VLF—confirming that ~7-min (420 s) recordings fully satisfy requirements for HF, LF, RMSSD, and SDNN while VLF remains near the minimum cycle boundary.
device: Clinical pulse wave / ECG HRV analyzer
reference_standard: Task Force standard 5-min (300 s) HRV recording from the same session
agreement_metric: Pearson correlation r, Kruskal-Wallis non-significant distribution test (p > 0.05), and Bland-Altman limits of agreement defining minimum valid durations (20 s HF, 30 s RMSSD, 90 s LF, 240 s SDNN, 270 s VLF)

citation: Munoz ML, van Roon A, Riese H, Thio C, Oostenbroek E, Westrik I, de Geus EJC, Gansevoort R, Lefrandt J, Nolte IM, Snieder H. Validity of (Ultra-)Short Recordings for Heart Rate Variability Measurements. PLoS One. 2015;10(9):e0138921.
design: Large population-based epidemiological validation study (n=3387 adults from PREVEND cohort)
signal_type: Supine resting beat-to-beat interbeat interval (IBI) series segmented into 10 s, 30 s, and 120 s windows vs 240-300 s criterion
decomposition: Time-domain beat-to-beat variance decomposition (SDNN and RMSSD on raw and log-transformed scales)
parameters_reported: SDNN and RMSSD across 10 s, 30 s, 120 s, and 240-300 s windows; Pearson r, ICC, Bland-Altman bias/LoA, and Cohen's d
sampling_resampling: Beat-to-beat R-peak detection and artifact correction in CARSPAN without interpolation
band_definitions: RMSSD (vagal HF 0.15-0.40 Hz variability) and SDNN (total beat-to-beat variability across window)
key_finding: In 3,387 adults, 120-s recordings achieved near-perfect agreement with standard 240-300 s recordings for both RMSSD (r = 0.986, Cohen's d = 0.027) and SDNN (r = 0.956, Cohen's d = 0.137), and even 30-s windows were valid for RMSSD (r > 0.90).
device: Portapres / laboratory ECG beat-to-beat acquisition (CARSPAN)
reference_standard: Standard 240-300 s (4-5 min) supine resting ECG recording
agreement_metric: At 120 s: RMSSD r = 0.986 (bias = 0.014, Cohen's d = 0.027), SDNN r = 0.956 (bias = 0.064, Cohen's d = 0.137)

citation: Shaffer F, Ginsberg JP. An Overview of Heart Rate Variability Metrics and Norms. Front Public Health. 2017;5:258.
design: Authoritative methodological review and normative synthesis of 24-h, short-term (~5 min), and ultra-short-term (<5 min) HRV
signal_type: ECG and PPG interbeat interval (IBI / NN) time series across 24-h, 5-min, and <5-min recording paradigms
decomposition: Time-domain, FFT / autoregressive (AR) / Lomb-Scargle frequency-domain, and nonlinear (Poincaré SD1/SD2, ApEn, SampEn, DFA alpha1/alpha2) analysis
parameters_reported: Normative ranges, physiological origins, and minimum recording durations for SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50, ULF, VLF, LF, HF, LF/HF, SD1, SD2, SampEn, DFA
sampling_resampling: Documents both cubic spline resampling (typically 4 Hz) for FFT/AR/HHT and Lomb-Scargle periodogram analysis directly on unevenly sampled IBI series
key_finding: Synthesizes physiological mechanisms and minimum window lengths for all HRV bands, establishing that ~5-10 min recordings reliably resolve HF (0.15-0.40 Hz) and LF (0.04-0.15 Hz) oscillations, whereas VLF (0.0033-0.04 Hz, period up to 300 s) contains <2-3 cycles in <10-min recordings and cannot be interchangeably compared with 24-h norms.
device: Clinical Holter ECG, short-term ECG, and wearable IBI sensors
reference_standard: Task Force of the European Society of Cardiology and the North American Society of Pacing and Electrophysiology (1996) standards
agreement_metric: Normative reference intervals and minimum duration thresholds (>=60 s HF, >=120 s LF, >=300 s VLF, 24 h ULF)

citation: Pecchia L, Castaldo R, Montesinos L, Melillo P. Are ultra-short heart rate variability features good surrogates of short-term ones? State-of-the-art review and recommendations. Healthc Technol Lett. 2018;5(3):94-100.
design: Systematic methodological review of 29 ultra-short-term HRV validation studies plus empirical stress-detection case study
signal_type: Ultra-short-term (<5 min: 10 s to 240 s) vs short-term (5 min) ECG and wearable PPG RR interval series
decomposition: Time-domain, frequency-domain (PSD / Lomb-Scargle), and nonlinear entropy (ApEn, SampEn) surrogate validity framework
parameters_reported: Validity hierarchy across time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear features as window length decreases below 300 s
sampling_resampling: Evaluates 4 Hz cubic spline resampling vs unevenly sampled Lomb-Scargle estimation and sample-count sensitivity for nonlinear entropy
key_finding: Revealed that 28 of 29 published ultra-short HRV studies relied on incomplete statistical tests and demonstrated that rigorous surrogate validation requires concurrent correlation, Bland-Altman bias/LoA, and preservation of group effect size across physiological states.
device: Wearable PPG / mobile ECG / ambulatory ECG systems across 29 reviewed studies
reference_standard: Standard 5-min (300 s) Task Force HRV recordings
agreement_metric: Three-tier validation protocol: Spearman r >= 0.70, non-significant Bland-Altman bias with narrow LoA, and concordant Cliff's delta effect size

citation: Rothberg LJ, Lees T, Clifton-Bligh R, Lal S. Association Between Heart Rate Variability Measures and Blood Glucose Levels: Implications for Noninvasive Glucose Monitoring for Diabetes. Diabetes Technol Ther. 2016;18(6):366-376.
design: Observational case-control study in patients with diabetes (n=32) and healthy controls (n=31; total n=63) during fasting and 30-min postprandial states
signal_type: 10-min 3-lead ECG (2048 Hz) RR interval series paired with capillary blood glucose measurements
decomposition: Welch Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) power spectral density and time-domain HRV analysis (Kubios HRV)
parameters_reported: LF power, HF power, Total Power (TP), LF/HF ratio, SDNN, RMSSD, and HR correlated against blood glucose levels
sampling_resampling: 2048 Hz 3-lead ECG R-peak extraction; 10-min RR series interpolated via cubic spline in Kubios for Welch PSD
key_finding: In diabetic participants, LF power, HF power, and Total Power were significantly negatively correlated with blood glucose concentration (and LF/HF ratio positively correlated), demonstrating direct coupling between acute glycemic levels and cardiac autonomic spectral power in 10-min recordings.
device: ADInstruments PowerLab 3-lead ECG (2048 Hz) and clinical glucometer
reference_standard: Simultaneous capillary blood glucose measurement (fasting and 30-min postprandial)
agreement_metric: Significant Pearson correlations (p < 0.05) between blood glucose and LF, HF, TP (negative) and LF/HF (positive) in diabetic cohort

citation: Jelinek HF, Tuladhar R, Culbreth G, Bohara G, Cornforth D, West BJ, Grigolini P. Diffusion Entropy vs. Multiscale and Rényi Entropy to Detect Progression of Autonomic Neuropathy. Front Physiol. 2021;11:607324.
design: Observational clinical complexity study across controls, borderline CAN, and definite CAN
signal_type: Beat-to-beat ECG RR interval time series
decomposition: Diffusion Entropy Analysis (DEA) detecting renewal 'crucial events' vs MSE and Rényi Entropy
parameters_reported: Scaling exponent delta and complexity index mu (healthy mu ~ 2.0 vs pathological mu -> 3.0), MSE, Rényi entropy
sampling_resampling: Un-interpolated beat-to-beat RR interval series mapped into continuous diffusion trajectories
band_definitions: Multiscale temporal scaling across short- and intermediate-term heartbeat fluctuations
key_finding: Demonstrated that healthy cardiac control operates in a perennial non-stationary complexity regime (mu ~ 2) and that diabetic autonomic neuropathy degrades renewal dynamics toward Gaussian stationary noise (mu -> 3), explaining why non-stationary methods outperform stationary linear HRV in diabetes.
device: Clinical lead-II ECG acquisition system
reference_standard: Ewing battery cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests
agreement_metric: Progressive shift of diffusion scaling exponent delta and complexity index mu from ~2.0 toward ~3.0

citation: Cheng W, Chen H, Tian L, Ma Z, Cui X. Heart rate variability in different sleep stages is associated with metabolic function and glycemic control in type 2 diabetes mellitus. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1157270.
design: Cross-sectional inpatient clinical cohort study in male patients with T2D (n=60, age 50 +/- 16 years)
signal_type: 24-hour single-lead ambulatory Holter ECG (250 Hz) segmented into awake and sleep stages
decomposition: Linear PSD + Nonlinear Entropy (ApEn, SampEn, FuzzyEn), DFA, MSE, and Multiscale Fuzzy Entropy (MFE) + ADF stationarity and surrogate testing
parameters_reported: SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50, VLF, LF, HF, LF/HF, ApEn, SampEn, FuzzyEn, DFA, MSE, MFE correlated against FBG, HbA1c, C-peptide, HOMA-IR
sampling_resampling: Holter ECG sampled at 250 Hz, filtered with 5-35 Hz bandpass filter, majority-vote R-peak detection across 4 detectors
band_definitions: HRV: VLF 0.00-0.04 Hz, LF 0.04-0.15 Hz, HF 0.15-0.40 Hz; CPC sleep bands: VLFC 0.003-0.01 Hz, LFC 0.01-0.1 Hz, HFC 0.1-0.4 Hz
key_finding: Proved via ADF and surrogate testing that diabetic sleep RR series are predominantly non-stationary and nonlinear (up to 68.42% in REM), and showed that sleep-stage nonlinear HRV metrics strongly correlate with glycemic control (DFA-alpha2 with FBG r = -0.584, p < 0.001; SampEn with HbA1c r = 0.438, p < 0.05), outperforming daytime and linear HRV.
device: 24-hour single-lead ambulatory Holter ECG recorder (250 Hz)
reference_standard: Inpatient venous metabolic panel (FBG, HbA1c, fasting C-peptide, 2-h postprandial C-peptide, HOMA-IR)
agreement_metric: DFA-alpha2 vs FBG r = -0.584; unstable sleep SampEn vs HbA1c r = 0.438; MSE5 vs HbA1c r = 0.442; 68.42% REM sleep RR segments nonlinear

citation: Cui X, Abduljalil A, Manor BD, Peng CK, Novak V. Multi-scale glycemic variability: a link to gray matter atrophy and cognitive decline in type 2 diabetes. PLoS One. 2014;9(1):e86284.
design: Cross-sectional observational study (n=43 older adults with T2D, n=26 controls; 72-h CGM, MRI, and cognitive battery)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (72-h CGM)
decomposition: Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (EEMD) into 5 intrinsic mode functions (GVC1-GVC5)
parameters_reported: EEMD cycle-specific SD and amplitudes across GVC1-GVC5; SD, MAGE, HbA1c, fasting glucose; regional GM volume and cognitive scores
period_range_claimed: 0.5-12.0 h across GVC1-GVC5 (GVC1-3 meal cycles 0.5-2.0 h; GVC3-5 ultradian/diurnal cycles 2.0-12.0 h)
sampling_interval: 5 min (72-h record; Nyquist period 10 min [6.0 cycles/h])
key_finding: Type 2 diabetes patients exhibited higher variability in 2.0-12.0 h EEMD cycles (GVC3-5, p < 0.0001) day and night; across all older adults, higher variability in fast 0.5-2.0 h cycles (GVC1-3) was independently associated with limbic/temporo-parietal gray matter atrophy and worse learning/memory scores independent of HbA1c and hypoglycaemia.

citation: Lai Y, Zhang Z, Li P, Liu X, Liu Y, Xin Y, Gu W. Investigation of glucose fluctuations by approaches of multi-scale analysis. Med Biol Eng Comput. 2018;56(3):505-514.
design: Observational cohort study in type 2 diabetes (n=98 stratified by MAGE > 3.9 vs <= 3.9 mmol/L; 72-h CGMS)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (72-h CGMS)
decomposition: Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (EEMD; IMFs 1-5) combined with Refined Composite Multiscale Entropy (RCMSE)
parameters_reported: IMF fluctuation amplitude (IMFs 1-5), RCMSE complexity across scale factors 1-6 (5-30 min), MAGE
period_range_claimed: 0.5-12.0 h for EEMD IMFs 1-5; 5-30 min coarse-grained scales for RCMSE
sampling_interval: 5 min (72-h record; Nyquist period 10 min)
key_finding: Patients with MAGE > 3.9 mmol/L showed significantly elevated glycemic variability specifically in slower EEMD modes (IMFs 3-5, periods ~2-12 h, p < 0.001) but not in fast modes (IMFs 1-2), accompanied by reduced RCMSE complexity across 5-30 min scales (p < 0.05).

citation: Patankar NM, Sanghvi SJ. Beyond Time in Range: Targeting Glucose Oscillations to Transform Vascular Outcomes in Diabetes. J Assoc Physicians India. 2026;74(6E):e39-e41.
design: Narrative review and conceptual framework synthesizing studies from 2002-2024
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (CGM)
decomposition: Conceptual Oscillatory Burden Index (OBI) combining amplitude and frequency metrics of intraday/postprandial CGM fluctuations
parameters_reported: TIR (70-80%), amplitude and frequency of intrarange glucose swings, CRP, ICAM-1, mitochondrial ROS, NF-kappaB
period_range_claimed: Intraday postprandial and ultradian oscillations (0.5-24.0 h)
sampling_interval: 1-5 min standard clinical CGM
key_finding: Patients with comparable TIR (70-80%) but high oscillatory amplitude/frequency burden exhibit 2-3-fold higher CRP and ICAM-1 levels (p < 0.05), underscoring that static range percentages mask vascular-damaging rhythmic glucose swings.

citation: Fleischer J, Lebech Cichosz S, Hoeyem P, Laugesen E, Loegstrup Poulsen P, Sandahl Christiansen J, Tarnow L, Hansen TK. Glycemic variability is associated with reduced cardiac autonomic modulation in women with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes Care. 2015;38(4):682-688.
design: Cross-sectional cohort study (n=87 newly diagnosed T2D: 48 men, 39 women; 72-h CGM and HRV/reflex testing)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (72-h CGM) paired with ECG RR intervals (HRV)
decomposition: MAGE for CGM; frequency-domain spectral power (LF, HF, TP) and time-domain (SDNN, RMSSD) for HRV
parameters_reported: CGM MAGE; HRV SDNN, RMSSD, LF power, HF power, LF/HF ratio, TP, cardiovascular reflex ratios
period_range_claimed: Intraday meal/ultradian excursions (1-12 h) paired with autonomic HRV LF (0.04-0.15 Hz) and HF (0.15-0.40 Hz)
sampling_interval: 5 min for CGM (72-h wear); millisecond RR intervals for ECG HRV
key_finding: In women with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, higher CGM glycemic variability (MAGE) was independently associated with reduced cardiac autonomic modulation across LF (p < 0.001), HF (p = 0.005), total power (p = 0.008), and SDNN (p = 0.001).

citation: Battelino T, Alexander CM, Amiel SA, Arreaza-Rubin G, Beck RW, Bergenstal RM, et al. Continuous glucose monitoring and metrics for clinical trials: an international consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2023;11(1):42-57.
design: International consensus statement and clinical trial reporting standard
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (transcutaneous/implantable CGM)
decomposition: None (time-marginalised distributional statistics, range percentages, and 24-h AGP percentile curves)
parameters_reported: TIR (3.9-10.0 mmol/L, target >70%), TITR, TBR Level 1 (<3.9 mmol/L, <4%) and Level 2 (<3.0 mmol/L, <1%), TAR Level 1 and 2, %CV (<=36%), SD, mean glucose, GMI, GRI, >=14 days wear with >=70% completeness
period_range_claimed: Diurnal vs nocturnal and 24-h aggregated profiles; explicitly notes that CV and SD do not quantify the frequency of glycemic oscillations. Sampling constraint: 5-min CGM Nyquist period = 10 min; 14-day record bounds slowest resolvable period to <= 104-112 h
sampling_interval: 1-5 min (14 consecutive days minimum recommended with >=70% completeness)
key_finding: Establishes the international clinical comparator set (TIR, TBR, TAR, CV, SD, GMI, GRI, 14-day AGP) while explicitly recognizing that standard metrics like CV collapse the time-frequency axis and do not measure the frequency of glycemic oscillations or within-/between-day modulation.

citation: Danne T, Nimri R, Battelino T, Bergenstal RM, Close KL, DeVries JH, et al. International Consensus on Use of Continuous Glucose Monitoring. Diabetes Care. 2017;40(12):1631-1640.
design: International consensus statement (ATTD Congress panel)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (rtCGM and isCGM)
decomposition: None (summary time-domain and time-in-range metrics, 14-day AGP modal day quantiles)
parameters_reported: TIR (70-180 mg/dL), TBR (<70 and <54 mg/dL), TAR (>180 and >250 mg/dL), %CV (<=36%), SD, eA1C/GMI, 14-day wear
period_range_claimed: 24-h modal-day aggregation and nocturnal vs daytime windows; no frequency-domain resolution
sampling_interval: 1-5 min (minimum 14 consecutive days with >=70% data capture)
key_finding: Defines %CV <= 36% as the primary time-domain threshold separating stable from labile glycemia and standardizes 14-day CGM wear as representative of 3-month glycemic exposure.

citation: Klonoff DC, Wang J, Rodbard D, Kohn MA, Li C, Liepmann D, et al. A Glycemia Risk Index (GRI) of Hypoglycemia and Hyperglycemia for Continuous Glucose Monitoring Validated by Clinician Ratings. J Diabetes Sci Technol. 2023;17(5):1226-1242.
design: Multicentre validation study (n=225 insulin-treated adults with diabetes; 14-day CGM tracings rated by 330 clinicians)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (14-day CGM)
decomposition: PCA and linear regression on 7 time-marginalised AGP range/variability metrics
parameters_reported: GRI, Hypoglycemia Component, Hyperglycemia Component, TIR, TBR (<54 and 54-69 mg/dL), TAR (>250 and 181-250 mg/dL), mean glucose, CV
period_range_claimed: 14-day aggregated time-in-range risk score (no spectral period resolution)
sampling_interval: 5 min over 14 consecutive days
key_finding: Clinician rankings of 14-day CGM quality are captured (r = 0.95) by a two-component composite score (GRI) weighting extreme hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, providing a single-number comparator that nonetheless omits oscillation frequency and modulation structure.

citation: Rodbard D. Glucose Variability: A Review of Clinical Applications and Research Developments. Diabetes Technol Ther. 2018;20(S2):S25-S215.
design: Comprehensive methodological and clinical review
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (CGM)
decomposition: Comparison of time-domain metrics (%CV, SD, MAGE, MODD, CONGA) with frequency and complexity methods (Fourier, periodograms, MSE, GVP)
parameters_reported: %CV, SD, MAGE, MODD, CONGA, Fourier harmonic amplitudes, periodogram power, MSE, GVP
period_range_claimed: Fast postprandial fluctuations (10-30 min via GVP) through ultradian (1-8 h) and circadian/diurnal (24 h) rhythms
sampling_interval: 5 min typical CGM (Nyquist period 10 min)
key_finding: Demonstrates that while SD and %CV are strongly collinear with amplitude metrics, frequency- and complexity-sensitive methods detect rapid closed-loop oscillations and progressive loss of dynamical complexity from normoglycemia to diabetes.

citation: Miller M, Strange P. Use of fourier models for analysis and interpretation of continuous glucose monitoring glucose profiles. J Diabetes Sci Technol. 2007;1(5):630-638.
design: Methodological and prospective clinical trial reanalysis
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (CGM)
decomposition: Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) harmonic regression and functional second-derivative analysis
parameters_reported: 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Fourier harmonic amplitudes and phases; second derivative; HbA1c; hypoglycemia
period_range_claimed: 24 h (1st harmonic), 12 h (2nd harmonic), and 8 h (3rd harmonic) circadian/ultradian periods
sampling_interval: 5 min (72-h CGM records; Nyquist period 10 min)
key_finding: Baseline 2nd (12-h) and 3rd (8-h) Fourier harmonic amplitudes of CGM profiles correlated with 6-month HbA1c response, and functional second derivatives identified points of rapid glucose descent predictive of hypoglycemia, though stationary sinusoids cannot track nonstationary meal timing.

citation: Penckofer S, Quinn L, Byrn M, Ferrans C, Miller M, Strange P. Does glycemic variability impact mood and quality of life? Diabetes Technol Ther. 2012;14(4):303-310.
design: Descriptive exploratory cohort study (n=23 women with type 2 diabetes; 72-h CGMS and mood/QoL questionnaires)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (72-h CGMS)
decomposition: Fourier statistical harmonic models (rate-of-change energy components) and CONGA-n
parameters_reported: 24-h SD, CONGA, Fourier harmonic energy components, HbA1c, depression/anxiety/QoL scores
period_range_claimed: 1-24 h intraday and circadian harmonic components over 72-h recording
sampling_interval: 5 min (72-h CGMS)
key_finding: Fourier energy components and steeper glucose excursion slopes on 72-h CGM were significantly associated with comorbid depression, higher trait anxiety, and lower quality of life in women with type 2 diabetes.

citation: Figueira FR, Umpierre D, Casali KR, Tetelbom PS, Henn NT, Ribeiro JP, Schaan BD. Aerobic and combined exercise sessions reduce glucose variability in type 2 diabetes: crossover randomized trial. PLoS One. 2013;8(3):e57733.
design: Randomized crossover trial (n=14 patients with T2D; 3-day CGMS across aerobic vs combined exercise)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (72-h CGMS)
decomposition: Power spectral analysis and non-linear symbolic dynamics (0V, 1V, 2LV, 2UV)
parameters_reported: SD, glucose variance, MAGE, %CV, spectral power, symbolic pattern frequencies (0V%, 1V%)
period_range_claimed: 15 min to 24 h post-exercise glycemic fluctuations
sampling_interval: 5 min (72-h CGMS)
key_finding: While conventional time-domain metrics showed no difference between exercise modalities over 24 h, non-conventional symbolic/spectral analysis detected a significant shift toward stable 0V patterns (67.0% to 76.0%, p = 0.003) and reduced 1V fluctuations (p = 0.004) after combined exercise.

citation: Kohnert KD, Heinke P, Vogt L, Augstein P, Thomas A, Salzsieder E. Associations of blood glucose dynamics with antihyperglycemic treatment and glycemic variability in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. J Endocrinol Invest. 2017;40(11):1201-1207.
design: Retrospective cross-sectional study (n=18 T1D, n=102 T2D, n=11 controls; 48-h CGM)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (CGM, n=576 samples per trace)
decomposition: Multiscale Entropy (MSE) coarse-graining analysis
parameters_reported: MSE complexity index, %CV, SD, mean glucose, HbA1c
period_range_claimed: 5-30 min coarse-grained temporal scales (scale factors 1-6 at 5-min sampling)
sampling_interval: 5 min (48-h record, n=576 points)
key_finding: The CGM multiscale entropy (MSE) complexity index was significantly lower in T2D than in controls and lowest in T1D (p < 0.001), correlating inversely with glycemic variability and antihyperglycemic therapy escalation.

citation: Kohnert KD, Heinke P, Vogt L, Augstein P, Salzsieder E. Applications of Variability Analysis Techniques for Continuous Glucose Monitoring Derived Time Series in Diabetic Patients. Front Physiol. 2018;9:1257.
design: Retrospective cross-sectional study (n=22 T1D, n=143 T2D, n=12 controls; 48-h CGM)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (48-h CGM)
decomposition: Poincaré plot geometry (SD1, SD2, SFE, AFE), DFA (alpha1, alpha2), and Multiscale Entropy (MSE)
parameters_reported: SD1, SD2, SFE, AFE, MSE index, DFA alpha1 and alpha2, %CV, SD, TIR
period_range_claimed: Short-term (5-60 min: SD1, MSE, DFA alpha1) vs longer-term (1-6 h: SD2, DFA alpha2) fluctuation regimes
sampling_interval: 5 min (48-h record, n=576 points; Nyquist period 10 min)
key_finding: Poincaré plot descriptors and DFA scaling exponents were significantly higher in T1D than T2D (p < 0.05) and dominated %CV in multivariable prediction of TIR, whereas standard coarse-grained MSE yielded mixed results on short 48-h records.

citation: Godat E, Preiser JC, Aude JC, Kalfon P. Dynamic properties of glucose complexity during the course of critical illness: a pilot study. J Clin Monit Comput. 2020;34(2):361-370.
design: Prospective ICU pilot study (n=10 critically ill patients with continuous central venous glucose monitoring)
signal_type: Central venous blood glucose (EIRUS continuous microdialysis sensor)
decomposition: Sliding-window (24-h overlapping intervals) Multiscale Entropy (MSE) and DFA
parameters_reported: Time-resolved MSE complexity index and DFA scaling exponent over overlapping 24-h windows
period_range_claimed: 1-60 min coarse-grained scales tracked dynamically across consecutive 24-h windows
sampling_interval: 1 min (continuous central venous sensor; Nyquist period 2 min)
key_finding: Splitting continuous 1-min ICU glucose recordings into overlapping 24-h windows revealed substantial nonstationary diurnal/clinical variations in glucose complexity (MSE) that are obscured by whole-stay summary indices.

citation: Hall H, Perelman D, Breschi A, Limcaoco P, Kellogg R, McLaughlin T, Snyder M. Glucotypes reveal new patterns of glucose dysregulation. PLoS Biol. 2018;16(7):e2005143.
design: Observational cohort and standardized meal-challenge study (n=57 adults wore Dexcom G4 CGM for 2-4 weeks)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (2-4 week CGM)
decomposition: Spectral clustering on complexity-invariant dynamic time warping (CID-DTW) distances of 2.5-h sliding windows
parameters_reported: Fraction of time in low, moderate, and severe variability glucotypes; postprandial excursion amplitude; OGTT, HbA1c
period_range_claimed: 2.5-h sliding windows capturing postprandial rhythms (0.5-4.0 h) across 14-28 day records
sampling_interval: 5 min (Dexcom G4; 2-4 weeks wear)
key_finding: Spectral clustering of 5-min CGM trajectories identified three glucotypes (low, moderate, severe variability) and revealed that clinically normoglycemic individuals spend 15% and 2% of time in prediabetic and diabetic glucose ranges during postprandial excursions.

citation: Wu Y, Feng K, Fu Y, Zhuo Q, Zheng M, Zhang H, Lin G, Liang X, Zhou X, Ji L, Zou X, Sun F. Unveiling glycaemic variability patterns linked to the triglyceride-glucose index in type 2 diabetes: Insights from continuous glucose monitoring. Diabetes Obes Metab. 2026;28(5):3752-3763.
design: Cross-sectional study (n=279 patients with T2D wearing 14-day CGM stratified by TyG index tertiles)
signal_type: Subcutaneous interstitial glucose (14-day CGM)
decomposition: Frequency-domain spectral analysis, circadian rhythm analysis, and spectral clustering with CID-DTW
parameters_reported: Time-domain (TIR, TAR, TBR, CV), frequency-domain spectral power (low- vs high-frequency), circadian parameters, TyG index
period_range_claimed: Low-frequency ultradian/circadian oscillations (4-24 h) vs high-frequency postprandial fluctuations (0.5-4 h)
sampling_interval: 5-15 min (14-day CGM record)
key_finding: Higher insulin resistance (TyG tertile) was associated with a paradoxical reduction in %CV (26.2% to 23.8%, p = 0.021) alongside a marked shift toward high-level, low-frequency glucose oscillations and severe variability glucotype (32.3% to 63.4%, OR = 1.87, p < 0.001).

citation: Simon C. Ultradian pulsatility of plasma glucose and insulin secretion rate: circadian and sleep modulation. Horm Res. 1998;49(3-4):185-190.
design: Human chronophysiological review and 24-h frequent venous sampling sleep-shift studies
signal_type: Venous plasma glucose and C-peptide-deconvolved insulin secretion rate (ISR)
decomposition: Pulse detection and time-series envelope/amplitude modulation analysis across sleep-wake and circadian cycles
parameters_reported: Rapid insulin pulse period (~10 min), ultradian glucose/ISR period (50-100 min), amplitude modulation by circadian phase and sleep/GH
period_range_claimed: Rapid pulses (~10 min) superimposed on ultradian oscillations (50-100 min), amplitude-modulated by 24-h circadian and sleep cycles
sampling_interval: 10 min for 24-h ultradian profiling (1-2 min required for rapid 10-min pulses)
key_finding: Establishes that plasma glucose and insulin secretion oscillate at ultradian periods (50-100 min) whose amplitude—rather than frequency—is modulated by circadian rhythm and sleep, providing direct physiological grounding for nested carrier-envelope H(t, fc, fam) decomposition.

citation: Schmitz O, Rungby J, Edge L, Juhl CB. On high-frequency insulin oscillations. Ageing Res Rev. 2008;7(4):301-305.
design: Review of human high-frequency and ultradian insulin/glucose oscillation studies

decomposition: Time-series pulse deconvolution and spectral/autocorrelation periodicity analysis
parameters_reported: High-frequency pulse period (6-10 min), slow ultradian period (~140 min), pulsatile fraction (>=75%), pulse regularity

citation: Levy JC. Insulin signalling through ultradian oscillations. Growth Horm IGF Res. 2001;11 Suppl A:S17-S23.

signal_type: Plasma glucose and insulin time series during basal and exogenous glucose infusion

citation: Mejean L, Bicakova-Rocher A, Kolopp M, Villaume C, Levi F, Debry G, Reinberg A, Drouin P. Circadian and ultradian rhythms in blood glucose and plasma insulin of healthy adults. Chronobiol Int. 1988;5(3):227-236.

citation: Van Cauter E, Shapiro ET, Tillil H, Polonsky KS. Circadian modulation of glucose and insulin responses to meals: relationship to cortisol rhythm. Am J Physiol. 1992;262(4 Pt 1):E467-E475.
design: Controlled crossover study in healthy adults (n=8; 24-h profiling with identical meals every 6 h or 12 h)
signal_type: Venous plasma glucose, serum insulin, C-peptide, and plasma cortisol

citation: Boden G, Ruiz J, Urbain JL, Chen X. Evidence for a circadian rhythm of insulin secretion. Am J Physiol. 1996;271(2 Pt 1):E246-E252.

key_finding: Under constant clamped glycemia over 68 h (nearly 3 circadian cycles), human insulin secretion rate exhibits an endogenous ~24-h circadian oscillation peaking between 12:00 and 18:00 and reaching a nadir between 00:00 and 06:00, anti-phase to melatonin.

citation: Stenvers DJ, Scheer FAJL, Schrauwen P, la Fleur SE, Kalsbeek A. Circadian clocks and insulin resistance. Nat Rev Endocrinol. 2019;15(2):75-89.
design: Authoritative mechanistic and clinical review
signal_type: Systemic glucose, insulin sensitivity, and central (SCN) vs peripheral tissue clock gene rhythms

citation: Phillips NE, Mareschal J, Biancolin AD, Sinturel F, Umwali S, Blanc S, et al. The metabolic and circadian signatures of gestational diabetes in the postpartum period characterised using multiple wearable devices. Diabetologia. 2025;68(2):419-432.

sampling_interval: 5-15 min CGM over 14 consecutive days

citation: Tsameret S, Froy O, Matz Y, Landau Z, Twito O, Wainstein J, Avital-Cohen N, Chapnik N, Jakubowicz D. citation: Reutrakul S, Simon SL, Wang Q, Manoogian ENC, Panda S, Ryu S, Gao Z, Griffiths C, Helgeson E, Mashek DG, Oldenburg N, Chow LS. citation: Tingley D, McClain K, Kaya E, Carpenter J, Buzsáki G. A metabolic function of the hippocampal sharp wave-ripple. Nature. 2021;597(7874):82-86.

parameters_reported: Ripple band 140-200 Hz, bundling intervals, ~10 min lag to glucose drop, lateral septum DREADD suppression
key_finding: Clustered hippocampal CA1 sharp wave-ripples (SWRs) reliably predict a transient decrease in peripheral interstitial glucose concentration after ~10 min, independent of circadian, ultradian, or meal-triggered rhythms; optogenetic CA1 ripples reproduce the glucose drop and pharmacogenetic inhibition of lateral septum abolishes it.

citation: Buzsáki G, Tingley D. Cognition from the Body-Brain Partnership: Exaptation of Memory. Annu Rev Neurosci. 2023;46:191-210.
design: Narrative and theoretical review
signal_type: Hippocampal theta and sharp wave-ripple (SWR) oscillations, hypothalamic-autonomic outputs, and systemic glucose dynamics
decomposition: Conceptual multiscale oscillatory hierarchy (nested slow endocrine/metabolic rhythms and fast hippocampal sequences)
parameters_reported: Temporal scales spanning milliseconds (ripples ~150 Hz) to minutes/hours (ultradian/metabolic glucose fluctuations)
key_finding: Proposes that cognitive memory and planning circuits evolved via exaptation of older homeostatic brain-body regulatory algorithms, with hippocampal SWRs serving a dual role in offline memory replay and systemic glycemic/endocrine regulation across sleep and quiet wakefulness.

citation: Buzsáki G. Hippocampal sharp wave-ripple: A cognitive biomarker for episodic memory and planning. Hippocampus. 2015;25(10):1073-1188.
design: Comprehensive review
signal_type: Hippocampal CA3-CA1 SPW-R local field potentials, neocortical slow oscillations, sleep spindles, and hypothalamic outputs

key_finding: Establishes SPW-Rs as an intrinsic nested oscillation (CA3-driven slow sharp-wave depolarization modulating fast CA1 ripple amplitude) that coordinates neocortical memory consolidation during NREM sleep and projects to subcortical/hypothalamic nuclei to influence neuroendocrine regulation.

citation: Hallschmid M, Born J. A brain signal that coordinates thought with metabolism. Nature. 2021;597(7874):39-40.
design: News and Views commentary / mechanistic perspective
signal_type: Hippocampal sharp wave-ripples, lateral septum-hypothalamic autonomic pathways, and peripheral blood glucose
decomposition: Event-triggered temporal coupling analysis
parameters_reported: ~10-minute latency between hippocampal SWR bursts and systemic blood glucose decrease
key_finding: Synthesizes how hippocampal SWR bursts act as a neuro-metabolic command signal routed via lateral septum and hypothalamus to lower peripheral glucose, hypothesizing that disturbed slow-wave sleep and ripple generation contribute to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes in aging.

citation: Yang X, Fedumenti FT, Niethard N, Hallschmid M, Born J, Rauss K. Regulation of peripheral glucose levels during human sleep. Sleep. 2025;48(6):zsaf042.
design: Human observational sleep study (n=10 healthy adults, 2 consecutive nights of simultaneous PSG and CGM)
signal_type: Scalp EEG (slow oscillations, sleep spindles, REM transitions) and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM, 1 sample/min)

key_finding: Translates the rodent SWR-glucose link to healthy humans: thalamocortical sleep spindles (which nest with hippocampal ripples) precede a robust decrease in peripheral interstitial glucose within 1-6 min, whereas slow oscillations precede glucose increases (5-11 min lag) and REM transitions precede glucose decreases (10-14 min lag).

citation: Lun Y, Hallschmid M, Born J, Niethard N. The influence of peripheral glucose on sleep brain oscillations. Sleep. 2025;48(11):zsaf151.
design: Experimental rodent crossover study (glucose injection vs water; 6-h fasting vs ad libitum) with concurrent skull EEG, CA1 LFP, and CGM
signal_type: Cortical EEG (slow oscillations, spindles), hippocampal CA1 LFP (sharp wave-ripples), and interstitial glucose

parameters_reported: 6-h post-intervention sleep window; SO-spindle PAC phase angle; ripple, spindle, and SO event densities
key_finding: Demonstrates bidirectional brain-glucose feedback during sleep: hippocampal ripples and cortical spindles precede transient peripheral glucose dips, while systemic glucose administration increases spindle density and 6-h fasting increases ripples, spindles, SOs, and shifts the preferred phase of SO-spindle PAC.

citation: Wirt RA, Crew LA, Ortiz AA, McNeela AM, Flores E, Kinney JW, Hyman JM. Altered theta rhythm and hippocampal-cortical interactions underlie working memory deficits in a hyperglycemia risk factor model of Alzheimer's disease. Commun Biol. 2021;4(1):1036.

citation: Ramirez-Villegas JF, Logothetis NK, Besserve M. Diversity of sharp-wave-ripple LFP signatures reveals differentiated brain-wide dynamical events. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2015;112(46):E6379-E6387.
design: Simultaneous hippocampal CA1 LFP and whole-brain BOLD fMRI in non-human primates (macaques)
signal_type: Hippocampal CA1 LFP (sharp-wave-ripple complexes) and whole-brain hemodynamic/metabolic BOLD fMRI

parameters_reported: Four SPW-R subtypes defined by ripple-to-sharp-wave phase alignment; SPW-R-triggered BOLD modulation maps

citation: Richter CG, Babo-Rebelo M, Schwartz D, Tallon-Baudry C. Phase-amplitude coupling at the organism level: The amplitude of spontaneous alpha rhythm fluctuations varies with the phase of the infra-slow gastric basal rhythm. Neuroimage. 2017;146:951-958.

key_finding: Demonstrates organism-level phase-amplitude coupling in humans: the phase of the intrinsic infra-slow gastric rhythm (~0.05 Hz) modulates the amplitude envelope of resting cortical alpha (10-11 Hz) in insular and occipito-parietal cortex via ascending visceral signaling.

citation: Todd J, Cardellicchio P, Swami V, Cardini F, Aspell JE. Weaker implicit interoception is associated with more negative body image: Evidence from gastric-alpha phase amplitude coupling and the heartbeat evoked potential. Cortex. 2021;143:254-266.

parameters_reported: Gastric-alpha PAC modulation index and HEP amplitude correlated with body image scores
key_finding: Replicates resting gastric-alpha phase-amplitude coupling in scalp EEG and shows that weaker gastric-alpha PAC and altered heartbeat-evoked potentials independently track diminished implicit interoceptive processing in humans.

citation: Balasubramani PP, Walke A, Grennan G, Perley A, Purpura S, Ramanathan D, Coleman TP, Mishra J. Simultaneous Gut-Brain Electrophysiology Shows Cognition and Satiety Specific Coupling. Sensors (Basel). 2022;22(23):9242.

parameters_reported: EGG normogastric phase (~0.05 Hz) to fronto-central EEG amplitude coupling across rest vs working memory and fasting vs satiety
key_finding: Gut-brain EGG-EEG phase-amplitude coupling is dynamically modulated by both metabolic state (fasting hunger vs satiety) and cognitive load (rest vs working memory), with left fronto-central PAC strength correlating with working memory accuracy.

citation: Kluger DS, Gross J. Respiration modulates oscillatory neural network activity at rest. PLoS Biol. 2021;19(11):e3001457.

signal_type: Whole-brain source-reconstructed MEG (2-150 Hz) and respiratory signal (~0.2-0.3 Hz)
decomposition: Spectral decomposition and PAC (respiratory phase to neural amplitude across delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma)
parameters_reported: Modulation index across 2-150 Hz carrier frequencies and whole-brain parcellation
key_finding: Provides a whole-brain human atlas of respiration-modulated brain oscillations (RMBOs), showing that slow respiratory phase cyclically modulates the amplitude of delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma oscillations across canonical networks.

citation: Tort ABL, Brankačk J, Draguhn A. Respiration-Entrained Brain Rhythms Are Global but Often Overlooked. Trends Neurosci. 2018;41(4):186-197.
design: Methodological and mechanistic review

decomposition: Linear bandpass filtering, Fourier/wavelet coherence, and phase-amplitude comodulograms
parameters_reported: Rodent respiratory rate (1-4 Hz rest, 4-12 Hz sniffing) and modulated fast gamma subband (70-120 Hz)
key_finding: Demonstrates that nasal respiration entrains slow LFP oscillations and strongly modulates 70-120 Hz gamma amplitude, warning that unmonitored respiratory rhythms frequently masquerade as intrinsic delta-gamma or theta-gamma PAC in standard linear comodulograms.

citation: González J, Cavelli M, Mondino A, Castro-Zaballa S, Brankačk J, Draguhn A, Torterolo P, Tort ABL. Breathing modulates gamma synchronization across species. Pflugers Arch. 2023;475(1):49-63.

signal_type: Electrocorticography (ECoG), olfactory bulb LFP, and concurrent respiration recordings
decomposition: Bandpass filtering, Hilbert PAC, and phase-locking value
parameters_reported: Species-specific respiration-modulated gamma carrier bands: mice 90-130 Hz, rats 60-100 Hz, cats 30-60 Hz
key_finding: Across mice, rats, and cats, the slow respiratory cycle phase-modulates both local cortical gamma amplitude and long-range olfactory-frontal gamma synchronization, with the carrier gamma frequency scaling inversely with brain size.

citation: Heck DH, McAfee SS, Liu Y, Babajani-Feremi A, Rezaie R, Freeman WJ, Wheless JW, Papanicolaou AC, Ruszinkó M, Sokolov Y, Kozma R. Breathing as a Fundamental Rhythm of Brain Function. Front Neural Circuits. 2017;10:115.

decomposition: Phase-locking and cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling
parameters_reported: Respiratory fundamental frequencies (~0.2-0.3 Hz humans, 1-10 Hz rodents) modulating fast cortical gamma activity
key_finding: Synthesizes evidence that respiration provides a continuous interoceptive and olfactory clock that modulates the amplitude envelope of fast cortical oscillations, organizing distributed neural assemblies across the brain.

citation: Väyrynen T, Helakari H, Korhonen V, Tuunanen J, Huotari N, Piispala J, Kallio M, Raitamaa L, Kananen J, Järvelä M, Matias Palva J, Kiviniemi V. citation: Väyrynen T, Helakari H, Korhonen V, Tuunanen J, Huotari N, Kananen J, Ebrahimi SM, Elabasy A, Järvelä M, Hautamäki K, Laurén K, Raitamaa L, Salmi U, Piispala J, Kallio M, Kiviniemi V. citation: Sargent KS, Martinez EL, Reed AC, Guha A, Bartholomew ME, Diehl CK, Chang CS, Salama S, Popov T, Thayer JF, Miller GA, Yee CM. Oscillatory Coupling Between Neural and Cardiac Rhythms. Psychol Sci. 2024;35(5):517-528.

parameters_reported: HF-HRV (0.15-0.40 Hz) phase coupling with EEG delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma amplitudes; directional Granger causality
key_finding: Demonstrates robust resting phase-amplitude coupling between vagally mediated HF-HRV phase and scalp EEG oscillatory amplitudes across all canonical frequency bands in healthy adults, with Granger causality indicating predominantly ascending heart-to-brain drive for delta through beta bands.

citation: Liao Q, Dai Z, Pei C, Zhang H, Hua L, Sheng J, Zhou H, Yao Z, Lu Q. Increased Modulation of Low-Frequency Cardiac Rhythms on Resting-State Left Insula Alpha Oscillations in Major Depressive Disorder: Evidence from a Magnetoencephalography Study. J Neurosci. 2025;45(14):e1327242025.

parameters_reported: HRV-LF (0.04-0.15 Hz) modulating phase; cortical alpha (~10 Hz) modulated amplitude in insula and pars triangularis
key_finding: Shows that the phase of low-frequency cardiac autonomic rhythms (HRV-LF, 0.04-0.15 Hz) significantly modulates 10 Hz MEG alpha amplitude in the human insula, and that sympathetic-dominated HRV-LF-to-left-insula-alpha PAC is pathologically elevated in major depressive disorder.

citation: Lyu J, Yeh CH, Shi W, Penzel T. Dynamic brain-heart interaction in sleep characterized by variational phase-amplitude coupling framework. Commun Biol. 2025;8(1):1235.

parameters_reported: HRV-LF (0.04-0.15 Hz) and HRV-HF (0.15-0.4 Hz) coupling with EEG delta (0.5-4 Hz) across sleep stages; surrogate validation
key_finding: Introduces a nonlinear/nonstationary adaptive decomposition (VMD-PAC) framework for brain-heart coupling, demonstrating that slow cortical EEG delta oscillations couple strongly with both HRV-LF and HRV-HF components during sleep, with OSA patients exhibiting altered coupling patterns.

citation: Schiecke K, Schmidt C, Piper D, Putsche P, Feucht M, Witte H, Leistritz L. Assignment of Empirical Mode Decomposition Components and Its Application to Biomedical Signals. Methods Inf Med. 2015;54(5):461-473.

decomposition: Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) with Kuhn-Munkres Algorithm (KMA) optimal IMF assignment and Hilbert cross-frequency coupling

citation: Stankovski T, Petkoski S, Raeder J, Smith AF, McClintock PV, Stefanovska A. Alterations in the coupling functions between cortical and cardio-respiratory oscillations due to anaesthesia with propofol and sevoflurane. Philos Trans A Math Phys Eng Sci. 2016;374(2067):20150186.

design: Retrospective multi-center case-control study (21 SUDEP vs 21 non-SUDEP controls; 76 generalized seizures)
signal_type: Ictal single-lead/clinical ECG and concurrent video-EEG
decomposition: Continuous wavelet transform (CWT) and PAC (respiratory 0.1-0.55 Hz phase modulating cardiac 0.7-3.7 Hz amplitude)
parameters_reported: 20-s sliding windows; 3x3 PAC frequency grid spanning respiratory 0.1-0.55 Hz and cardiac 0.7-3.7 Hz; ROC AUC = 0.91
key_finding: Shows that cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling between respiratory (0.1-0.55 Hz) and cardiac (0.7-3.7 Hz) oscillations extracted directly from ictal ECG distinguishes SUDEP from non-SUDEP epilepsy patients with 91% AUC.

citation: Jelinek HF, Alkhodari M, Khandoker AH, Hadjileontiadis LJ. Oscillatory components of bidirectional cardio-respiratory coupling in depression and suicidal ideation: insights from swarm decomposition and entropy analysis. Front Netw Physiol. 2025;5:1620862.
design: Human clinical case-control study (n=74: 35 controls, 21 MDD without suicidal ideation, 18 MDD with suicidal ideation)
signal_type: Simultaneous resting ECG, finger PPG, and respiration (2-min segments)
decomposition: Adaptive Swarm Decomposition (SwD) into four oscillatory components (OC1-OC4) with Hilbert phase synchronization and entropy
parameters_reported: 2-min resting recordings; 4 adaptive oscillatory modes (OC1-OC4); Higuchi/Katz fractal dimension; phase-coupling index
key_finding: Applies nonlinear adaptive Swarm Decomposition (SwD) to isolate intrinsic oscillatory modes of cardiovascular and respiratory signals in short 2-min recordings, revealing frequency-specific disruptions in bidirectional cardiorespiratory phase coupling and reduced complexity in suicidal ideation.

citation: Klimesch W. The frequency architecture of brain and brain body oscillations: an analysis. Eur J Neurosci. 2018;48(7):2431-2453.
design: Theoretical synthesis and mathematical scaling analysis
signal_type: Brain rhythms (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma) and body rhythms (heart rate, HRV, respiration, gastric, BOLD)
decomposition: Binary frequency-doubling hierarchy (f_n = 2^n f_0) governed by m:n phase-to-envelope and harmonic phase-to-phase coupling
parameters_reported: Center frequencies across 12 octaves spanning infra-slow body oscillations (~0.01-1 Hz) to fast cortical oscillations (1-150 Hz)
key_finding: Formulates the Binary Hierarchy Brain-Body Oscillation Theory, proposing that brain and peripheral body rhythms form a single octave-scaled coupled system governed by phase-to-envelope (amplitude modulation) and harmonic phase-to-phase coupling.

citation: Bashan A, Bartsch RP, Kantelhardt JW, Havlin S, Ivanov PCh. Network physiology reveals relations between network topology and physiological function. Nat Commun. 2012;3:702.
design: Human polysomnographic physiological network study across wake, REM, light sleep, and deep sleep
signal_type: Simultaneous multi-organ recordings: scalp EEG (delta, theta, alpha, sigma, beta), ECG heart rate, respiration, chin EMG, and EOG
decomposition: Sliding-window spectral power / amplitude extraction and Time Delay Stability (TDS) cross-correlation across organ pairs
parameters_reported: 30-s windows; lag stability threshold across 5 EEG bands and peripheral cardiac, respiratory, ocular, and muscular series
key_finding: Establishes the field of Network Physiology by demonstrating that human physiological states (wake, REM, light and deep sleep) are uniquely defined by the topological network of time-delayed amplitude couplings across brain, cardiac, respiratory, and muscular systems.

citation: Bartsch RP, Liu KK, Bashan A, Ivanov PCh. Network Physiology: How Organ Systems Dynamically Interact. PLoS One. 2015;10(11):e0142143.
design: Human nocturnal polysomnography cohort study (n=36 healthy young adults)
signal_type: Continuous EEG (delta, theta, alpha, sigma, beta across frontal, central, occipital sites), ECG HR, respiration, chin/leg EMG, EOG
decomposition: Moving-window Fourier band power and Time Delay Stability (TDS) network mapping across frequency-specific links
parameters_reported: 30-s windows with 15-s step; 60-s TDS stability window; frequency-resolved coupling matrices across sleep stages
key_finding: Constructs the first frequency-resolved atlas of human multi-organ interactions, showing that brain-heart and brain-respiration couplings are mediated through distinct EEG frequency channels (e.g., gamma/beta in wake/REM vs delta/theta in NREM) and reorganize hierarchically.

citation: Lin A, Liu KK, Bartsch RP, Ivanov PCh. Delay-correlation landscape reveals characteristic time delays of brain rhythms and heart interactions. Philos Trans A Math Phys Eng Sci. 2016;374(2067):20150182.
design: Human nocturnal sleep EEG-ECG coupling study (n=34 healthy subjects)
signal_type: Synchronized continuous scalp EEG (delta, theta, alpha, sigma, beta power envelopes) and ECG instantaneous heart rate
decomposition: Time-resolved band-power amplitude envelopes and Delay-Correlation Landscape (DCL) analysis
parameters_reported: Characteristic time-delay probability distributions between EEG amplitude modulations and heart rate bursts across sleep stages
key_finding: Shows that amplitude envelope modulations of cortical EEG rhythms and cardiac rate fluctuations share universal time-delay profiles across healthy humans, with the direction and delay distribution shifting systematically across wake, REM, light sleep, and deep sleep.

citation: Ivanov PC. The New Field of Network Physiology: Building the Human Physiolome. Front Netw Physiol. 2021;1:711778.
design: Foundational field perspective / review

parameters_reported: Multiscale temporal hierarchy from milliseconds to circadian cycles across coupled organ networks
key_finding: Defines the Human Physiolome agenda, arguing that physiological health and disease cannot be reduced to single-organ metrics because essential regulatory information resides in transient cross-frequency phase and amplitude-envelope couplings across organ systems.

citation: Romero-Ortuño R, Martínez-Velilla N, Sutton R, Ungar A, Fedorowski A, Galvin R, Theou O, Davies A, Reilly RB, Claassen J, Kelly ÁM, Ivanov PC. Network Physiology in Aging and Frailty: The Grand Challenge of Physiological Reserve in Older Adults. Front Netw Physiol. 2021;1:712430.

citation: Garcia-Retortillo S, Abenza Ó, Ma YJX, Thiamwong L, Posada-Quintero H, Pinzon-Arenas J, Leinbach C, Fukuda DH, Ivanov PC. Network integration and evolution of organ systems interactions during incremental exercise. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2026;10.1007/s00421-026-06401-8.
design: Prospective human physiological study (n=26 healthy young adults performing graded cycling test to exhaustion)
signal_type: Synchronized bilateral vastus lateralis and erector spinae EMG, 3-lead ECG, and thoracic respiratory waveform
decomposition: Amplitude-Amplitude Cross-Frequency Coupling (ACFC) across cardio-muscular, respiratory-muscular, and inter-muscular networks
parameters_reported: Comparison of first third vs last third of incremental CPET; ~30% increase in Heart-Leg ACFC and ~50-75% increase in Respiration-Leg ACFC with exhaustion
key_finding: Demonstrates that progressive physiological stress reorganizes cross-frequency amplitude co-modulation across heart, lungs, and skeletal muscles in humans, increasing cardio-muscular (+30%) and respiratory-muscular (+50-75%) amplitude coupling as local neuromuscular fatigue develops.
